power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1 was used to help determine sample size before enrollment (Faul et al., 2007), resulting in N = 34 for a matched-pairs t test (two-tailed, dz = 0.50, α = .05, power = .80). We targeted 40 individuals anticipating a 15% attrition rate.

Of the 40 original participants enrolled, 85.0% (n = 34) completed T3. Seventeen participants missed the 6-month assessment window, leaving a sample of 23 (57.5% of baseline); of these 17, 11 had completed T3 and six had completed neither follow-up. Thus, the power analysis held for T3, but not for T6 where the 23 remaining participants allow for 80% power to detect effects of dz = 0.61 or larger. To test if there were significant differences in any of our outcome measures at T0, Welch's independent-samples t tests were run comparing T3 completers to non-completers on all seven clinical scales. These revealed no significant differences (all ps > .45). The same comparisons at 6 months showed no significant baseline differences (all ps > .06), but completers had higher baseline depression scores (PHQ-9; M = 11.87 vs. 8.24, d = 0.59, p = .065), PTSD severity (PCL-5; M = 39.96 vs. 28.00, d = 0.56, p = .075), anxiety (GAD-7; d = 0.42) and lower life satisfaction (SWLS; d = -0.51) than non-completers. Among participants who completed the 3-month assessment, those lost before 6 months had smaller 3-month improvements than those retained (PCL-5 of -5.2 vs. -13.0; PHQ-9 of -1.8 vs. -3.4) and fewer training sessions by 3 months (M = 23.1 vs. 32.0), although M2CQ change was similar (-5.6 in both groups).

text.text: Combat veterans experience higher incidences of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, along with challenges adjusting to life post-discharge, but have been under-served by traditional mental health treatments.
Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has emerged as potentially therapeutic for combat veterans, although empirical support is lacking.
A single-arm pre-post pilot study was used to evaluate seven psychosocial outcomes among participants from the We Defy Foundation program (N = 40; 87.5% male; Mage = 41.1, SD = 5.8).

Primary outcomes were self-reported post-traumatic stress severity (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; PCL-5), depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7; GAD-7), and military-to-civilian transition difficulty (Military to Civilian Questionnaire; M2CQ).

Secondary outcomes included Self-Efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), Functional Disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule; WHODAS 2.0), and Life Satisfaction (Satisfaction with Life Scale; SWLS).
Assessments were completed at baseline (T0; n = 40), 3 months (T3; n = 34), and 6 months (T6; n = 23).

Results revealed high symptom scores at baseline, with significant improvements in the four primary outcomes at both T3 (Cohen's dz = 0.52-0.63) and T6 (dz = 0.84-1.04) and seven of eight remained significant under Bonferroni correction.
GSE and SWLS improved significantly at T3, and SWLS and WHODAS at T6.

These preliminary findings suggest that BJJ participation may be associated with positive mental health improvements for the veteran population and provide a basis for future controlled studies investigating similar, complementary and alternative approaches.

After military service, many Americans carry at least one mental health diagnosis, with the most common being Post-traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), other anxiety disorder, and alcohol use disorder, with estimated prevalence rates of 28%, 22%, 12%, and 6%, respectively (Brancu et al., 2017; Department of Veterans Affairs & Department of Defense, 2016).

text.text: Several barriers exist for veteran care including stigma (e.g., the sentiment that therapy is for the weak), fear of adverse effects to employment/career advancement opportunities, distrust of civilian mental health systems, and a perceived cultural mismatch between the "patient" role and military identity.
These are largely reflected in lower initiation rates and dropout rates near 50% (Edwards-Stewart et al., 2021; Penix-Smith & Swift, 2025).

text.text: Collectively, these challenges point to the need for and value in developing interventions that carry the following characteristics: empirically supported, culturally relevant, accessible, and able to foster engagement for those veterans who either decline or fail to pursue traditional clinical mental health services (Seal et al., 2010).

text.text: The evidence basis for physical activity as a mental health intervention has grown substantially (Rebar et al., 2015; Rosenbaum et al., 2015), however, generic formats for resistance or aerobic training constitute the overwhelming majority of exercise programs in the literature.

text.text: These may be sound physiologically but miss opportunities to leverage related factors such as group cohesion, discipline, and a shared mission/challenge.

A robust complementary intervention for this group should offer not only physical activity but a framework consistent with military identity, a community emulating the kinship of service and a structure rewarding dedication.
The focus of this research is on one such possibility: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ).

BJJ is a sport and grappling-based martial arts system with roots in Japanese Judo, which focuses on positional control (e.g., having an opponent pinned) and submission techniques (e.g., joint manipulation resulting in an opponent "tapping out" to signal defeat) with emphasis on live sparring.

The infrastructure and ethos of modern BJJ practice maps onto much of military culture, containing: (1) a belt-rank hierarchy mirroring military rank structure, (2) physical rigor and shared hardship mirroring unit cohesion, and (3) technical mastery mirroring mission focus.
The training gym and community provide a "new unit" in the civilian world (Collura, 2018).
text.formatted: The training gym and community provide a "new unit" in the civilian world <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Collura, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This has long been recognized outside of academia by organizations like the We Defy Foundation (WDF).

Following the biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1980), we suggest several pathways through which BJJ may confer benefits beyond the well-documented benefits from vigorous physical exercise (Rebar et al., 2015), though testing these mechanisms was beyond the scope of this study.

text.text: First, BJJ carries a distinct culture of discipline, perseverance, and mutual respect mapping onto military values, and shared physical struggle may serve as a form of bonding that many veterans report losing upon separation from service.

Second, the technical complexity of BJJ demands problem solving under pressure, thereby building and relying on executive function, attentional control, and self-efficacy through the gradual acquisition of skill.

Third, training demands present-moment attention and graded exposure to physical closeness, while participants retain autonomy, which may interrupt ruminative cycles (Hsu et al., 2015) and offer a structured rehearsal of distress tolerance (Craske et al., 2014).

text.text: Fourth, the social membership inherent to the practice and shared experiences with fellow training partners promote connection and combat isolation.

Taken together, these pathways could support the (re)construction of a coherent identity after separation, which many veterans experience as an identity transition as much as an occupational one (Orazem et al., 2017).

text.text: The peer-reviewed research on this topic is sparse.
To date, only five articles in academic journals study mental health outcomes of BJJ in a veteran population, only three of which are empirical.

One review by Blomqvist Mickelsson (2021) included 12 articles that conceptualize BJJ as largely a psychosocial therapy and found a trend of a negative association between training experience and aggression.
The review by Segovia et al. (2024) highlighted that there is very little systematic research on the subject, and the studies that exist are limited by small, cross-sectional samples.

text.text: Of the three research studies that used longitudinal designs, Willing et al. (2019) investigated a 5month course of BJJ for 29 male US service members, but only 9 participants completed the study, showing improvements in symptoms of PTSD, depression, anxiety, and substance-use.

text.text: Both modalities showed improvements in anxiety, depression, PTSD, and sleep over a two-month time frame.

They also produced some unique insights based on qualitative interviews, which suggested BJJ participants more frequently connected their identities to the benefits of "constructive hardship" and community support.

The current pilot study attempts to fill this void using a single-arm pre-post longitudinal study design to evaluate changes in the following four primary outcome variables from Baseline (T0) to 3-Month (T3) and 6-Month (T6) follow-up in a group of veterans participating in a We Defy Foundation BJJ Program: PTSD symptom severity (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; PCL-5), depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7; GAD-7), and transition from military-to-civilian life (Military to Civilian Questionnaire; M2CQ).

Secondary outcomes assessed were self-efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), functional disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule; WHODAS 2.0), and satisfaction with life (Satisfaction with Life Scale; SWLS).

We had two main aims: first, to evaluate the change in the primary outcomes hypothesizing decreases in symptoms and difficulties at both follow-ups, and second, to evaluate secondary outcomes which we expected to improve similarly.
Linear mixed models using all enrolled participants supplement these analyses.
Exploratory aims included a direct comparison of 3-and 6-month outcomes, associations between training sessions and response, and sensitivity analyses addressing missing data and outlier influence.
We also describe feasibility based on retention and training attendance.
This study is framed as a single-arm pilot with the goal of providing preliminary estimates to inform a controlled trial and not to establish efficacy.

Participants were veterans recruited through the We Defy Foundation, a national nonprofit organization providing BJJ training scholarships and resources to combat veterans with serviceconnected disabilities.

This process involves a twice-yearly application cycle where veterans apply for the scholarship and We Defy assesses fit with the program and determines eligibility (which requires a VA disability rating of 80% or higher, having served in a combat zone, having an honorable discharge from the military, being separated or retired from active duty, being willing to train at least twice a week for one year, and being new to Jiu-Jitsu or a current white belt).
The study team did not independently verify all We Defy criteria.
Additional exclusions for the current study were inability to understand English and lack of access to a computer or phone with internet capability and videoconferencing software.
Participants enrolled between June and December 2025.

The study was approved by the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center Institutional Review Board (IRB) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki; all participants provided informed consent via videoconference and electronic signature.
Data were stored as coded study IDs on HIPAA-compliant platforms.

Procedure BJJ training was administered through We Defy Foundation "Approved Training Facilities" (currently numbering 1,209 across 50 States, 2 US Territories, Guam, and Japan), a classification awarded by the organization that recognizes gyms after having demonstrated safe and quality instruction (with teachers at the highest belt rank (black) and positive track records).
Sessions themselves were not standardized, but typically consisted of a structured warm-up, technical instruction and drilling, and live sparring (rolling) for 60-90 minutes.
Assessments took place at baseline and after 3 and 6 months (median of 96 and 187 days after baseline, respectively).

This first assessment window was chosen to mirror approximate length of care seen both in exercise-based interventions (Jadhakhan et al., 2022) as well as trauma-focused psychotherapy protocols (e.g., CPT or PE; (Schnurr et al., 2022) and the second was used to examine if changes continued with more training.

text.text: In this preliminary investigation, combat veterans with service-connected disabilities who engaged in BJJ reported improvements in psychiatric symptomatology and indices of wellbeing with six of seven outcomes improving by three months.
At six months, six of seven outcomes were also improved, and among participants who completed both follow-ups, PTSD, depression and anxiety symptoms continued to improve between T3 and T6.

Importantly, these results were found across not only the domains of psychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety, PTSD), but also functional wellbeing (life satisfaction, disability) and veteran-specific constructs (military-to-civilian transition).
Further, mixed models using all 40 enrolled participants showed the same pattern for the four primary outcomes.
Two factors distinguish our study over existing work.

First, positive findings on the M2CQ speak directly to transition-specific challenges in this population like relating to others, feeling belonging, finding meaning (Sayer et al., 2010), suggesting BJJ research may add to the literature on adjustment-related difficulties that generic exercise programs do not often measure.

text.text: These estimates are not directly comparable due to the uncontrolled sample in this study, but they make a case for a controlled trial.

Improvements may stem from several pathways including, repeated exposure to reduce avoidance and hyperarousal, a bodyfocused modality that addresses somatic symptoms, and a training environment structured to counter hypervigilance, but further research is needed to evaluate these possible mechanisms because they were not directly studied here.

The continued improvement in PTSD, depression, and anxiety symptoms (though not M2CQ scores) from T3 to T6 in our participants assessed at both follow-ups, rather than the plateau or reversal often seen in the exercise literature on depression, for example (e.g., Krogh et al., 2011), is a noticeable feature of these findings.

text.text: This pattern may reflect the framework proposed in the Introduction, though its mechanisms were not tested in this study: continued improvement may stem from processes seen in BJJ over time, such as technical skill accumulation, deeper social integration (e.g., relationships with training partners), and the solidifying of a reconstructed identity.

The M2CQ -without published and validated clinical cut-offs -is worth noting given the substantial effect sizes (T3 dz = 0.52; T6 dz = 0.84), but interpretation of change at the individual level is difficult.

Separation from service comes as a significant adjustment for many veterans, often distinct from psychiatric burden alone (Orazem et al., 2017; Zogas, 2017): a sense of social belonging may be lost alongside their rank and role within their unit, so approaches suited to address this gap merit further investigation.

text.text: One untested hypothesis is that a BJJ gym may be a viable option with its familiar rank structure, shared goals, and community based on closeness with training partners.

These processes may also make conventional care easier to approach or stay in, which is crucial because veterans have been shown to seek care less often, a pattern that hyperarousal, avoidance, general distrust may help explain (Bovin et al., 2019; Seal et al., 2010), and respond less well to first-line PTSD therapies (Milligan et al., 2025; Straud et al., 2019).

text.text: A veteran who is less reactive, with increased self-efficacy, and more connected with peers may find seeking or staying in treatment less costly.
This possibility was not examined here and would require measuring treatment engagement.
First and foremost, causal inference is impossible due to the lack of a control group (e.g., we cannot rule out natural recovery or non-specific effects).
Because concurrent treatment was not assessed, we cannot rule out possible contributions to change from psychotherapy, medications, peer support, or other exercise.
Regression to the mean is also always a possible contributor to results such as these, as participants with the highest baseline scores tended to improve the most.
As well, the small sample is a real limitation with wide confidence intervals around effect sizes requiring replication in a larger sample.
Next, the study recruitment pipeline relied on self-selection for participation in BJJ and likely reflects a positively-biased view towards the practice.
Participants with an aversion to contact sports were unlikely to enroll, as were the most severely or functionally impaired.
Also, the sample was predominantly male (though only slightly more proportionally when compared to the U.S. military), white, and well-educated, so results may not extend to other groups.

Retention at T6 was 57.5%, and there were no statistically significant differences between completers and non-completers on baseline clinical measures, but 6-month completers had moderately higher baseline depression and PTSD scores (d = 0.59 and 0.56).

Thus, T6 estimates may overstate change and futher investigation for dropout reasoning is warranted; the study team did not track program participation and could not distinguish discontinuation of training from loss to research follow-up.
Next, all variables were measured in a self-report fashion.

While this is a strength for understanding one's personal emotional experiences and appreciating their perspective on functioning, it has limitations, including susceptibility to demand characteristics of the study.

Finally, intervention delivery was heterogeneous; number of training sessions attended varied widely, instructors and facilities differed (though all were vetted), and attendance was measured by participant report.

This study represents a step towards understanding BJJ as a veteran mental health intervention by documenting multidimensional changes across symptoms, functioning, and transition outcomes in combat veterans with service-connected disabilities who trained, and by providing effect size estimates to plan a controlled trial.

Future studies should focus on (1) including an active control group, (2) longer follow-up intervals to examine longer-term trajectories, (3) inclusion of more diverse groups, (4) deploying physiological measures to track changes more directly (e.g., wearable technology to probe heartrate variability), (5) determining psychological and personality profiles to help identify bestresponders, as this martial art will not be appropriate for many, and (6) directly measuring the proposed mechanisms, such as social connectedness, military identity and treatment engagement.
To this end, the research team is examining longer-term outcomes and a future phase II controlled trial using physiological measurements.

While more empirical work is needed, service organizations and community partners should be encouraged by these results and continue reducing barriers to this and similar activities while controlled studies proceed.
BJJ may offer a community-based and culturally congruent option for reaching veterans who do not always engage with or benefit sufficiently from conventional mental health care.
For veterans who are physically able and psychologically willing to engage, BJJ may help reduce psychiatric symptom burden, and combat isolation and disconnection from purpose.
